prompt: In a simplified serial-refill model, a 256 KiB working set is entirely evicted from L2. Assume 64-byte cache lines and a hypothetical 20 ns per L3 refill, with no overlap. What is the sum of refill latencies?

options.explanation: This uses 256 lines. 256 KiB holds 256 × 1,024 / 64 = 4,096 lines, not 256.
That works for 1,000 lines. The working set is about four times that.
Correct. The supplied serial model sums 4,096 refills at 20 ns each to about 82 µs. It supplies no measurement of scheduler-switch time.
That would require more than 1 µs per line, inconsistent with the hypothetical 20 ns supplied here.

workedExample:
Count the cache lines, then add up the refill times:

```formula
N_lines = W / L
N_lines = (256 × 1,024 B) / 64 B
N_lines = 262,144 B / 64 B = 4,096
T = N_lines t_line
T = 4,096 × 20 ns = 81,920 ns
T ≈ 81.92 µs
where
N_lines: the number of cache lines the working set fills
W: the working set, 256 KiB = 262,144 bytes
L: the cache-line size, here 64 bytes
T: the total refill time if refills happen one after another
t_line: the hypothetical time to refill one line from L3, here 20 ns
B: byte
ns: nanosecond, one billionth of a second
µs: microsecond, one millionth of a second (1,000 ns)
≈: approximately equal to
In words: 4,096 lines refilled one at a time at 20 ns each add up to about 82 µs.
```

Real elapsed cost can differ because of prefetch, overlap, bandwidth and which lines are actually accessed.

prompt: After Meltdown, Linux enabled KPTI. Why did PCID support on the CPU become important for performance?

options.text: PCID encrypts kernel memory, which KPTI requires
options.explanation: PCID has nothing to do with encryption. It tags TLB entries with an address-space ID.

options.text: When enabled, KPTI switches page tables at user/kernel transitions; PCID can avoid full TLB flushing on those switches
options.explanation: Correct. With PCID, user and kernel translations carry different tags and survive the `CR3` writes, so syscalls don't start with a cold TLB.

options.text: PCID lets the kernel skip saving registers on syscalls
options.explanation: Registers are still saved on kernel entry. PCID only affects whether TLB entries survive a `CR3` load.

options.text: PCID stops the scheduler migrating tasks between cores
options.explanation: Migration is a scheduler decision. PCID is about TLB tagging on a single core.

workedExample: KPTI uses restricted user page tables and full kernel page tables. User/kernel transitions may switch between them. PCID can retain translations under different tags instead of invalidating non-global entries on every transition; invalidation is still required when mappings change. Actual performance benefit depends on workload and processor, not a fixed count of misses.
